content: Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) has been shown to be effective in term infants with hypoxic respiratory failure. However, the underlying mechanisms of respiratory failure and the associated risks of iNO differ significantly in preterm infants, necessitating specific investigation in this population. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of iNO treatment on mortality, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) or other severe brain injuries, and adverse long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes in preterm infants with hypoxic respiratory failure. Due to substantial variability in study eligibility criteria, the participants were divided into three groups for analysis: (1) infants treated within the first three days of life due to oxygenation defects, (2) preterm infants with pulmonary disease who received routine iNO treatment, and (3) infants treated after three days of age due to an elevated risk of developing BPD. The study employed standard methods of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group, searching databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, Healthstar, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials up to January 2016. Abstracts from the Pediatric Academic Societies were also reviewed. Eligible studies included randomized and quasi-randomized trials comparing iNO gas to control (with or without placebo) in preterm infants with respiratory disease. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Seventeen randomized controlled trials involving iNO therapy in preterm infants were identified. These trials were categorized post hoc into three groups based on entry criteria: early treatment within the first three days of life for oxygenation issues, routine use in preterm infants with respiratory support, and later treatment for infants at increased risk of BPD. No overall analyses were performed. Eight trials focusing on early rescue treatment for oxygenation issues showed no significant effect of iNO on mortality or BPD (risk ratio [RR] 0.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.87 to 1.01; 958 infants). Four studies investigating the routine use of iNO in preterm infants with pulmonary disease also demonstrated no significant reduction in death or BPD (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.02; 1924 infants), although the effect approached statistical significance. Later treatment with iNO for infants at increased risk of BPD, based on three trials, did not show a significant benefit for this outcome (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.01; 1075 infants). There was no clear evidence that iNO affected the incidence of IVH, including all grades and severe cases. Early rescue treatment was associated with a non-significant 20% increase in severe IVH. Additionally, no effect of iNO was observed on the incidence of neurodevelopmental impairment. In conclusion, iNO does not appear to be effective as a rescue therapy for critically ill preterm infants. Early routine use of iNO in preterm infants with respiratory disease does not prevent severe brain injury or improve survival without BPD. Later use of iNO to prevent BPD may have a small effect, but current evidence is inconclusive, and further research is needed to clarify its potential benefits.
